text:
IN
THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Nesbitt v. Neufeld,

2010 BCSC 42

Date: 20100113

Docket:
S118846

Registry: New Westminster

Between:

Patrick
Michael Nesbitt

Plaintiff

And

Wendy
Lee Neufeld

Defendant

Before: The Honourable Madam Justice Hyslop

Reasons for Judgment

Patrick
Michael Nesbitt appeared on his own behalf:

Counsel for the Defendant:

M.A. Misner

Place and Date of Hearing:

New Westminster, B.C.

November 24, 2009

Place and Date of Judgment:

New Westminster, B.C.

January 13, 2010

[
1
]

This application is brought by the defendant,
Wendy Lee Neufeld, to strike paragraphs 2 to 164 of the statement of claim
filed by the plaintiff, Patrick Michael Nesbitt (“Dr. Nesbitt”).  The
application is pursuant to Rules 1(5), 2(2)(d), 19(1), (9.1), (11), (12) and
Rule 32 of the
Rules of Court
(the “
Rules
”) and
s. 3(2)
of the
Limitation
Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 266.  Ms. Neufeld is seeking special costs.

[
2
]

After hearing submissions of Ms. Neufeld’s
counsel and those of Dr. Nesbitt, I allowed Ms. Neufeld’s application by
striking out paragraphs 2 to 164 of Dr. Nesbitt’s statement of claim.  I
ordered that if Dr. Nesbitt wished to pursue this proceeding that he amend his
statement of claim by December 8, 2009, and deliver a copy of the filed amended
statement of claim to Ms. Neufeld’s counsel no later than 12 noon on December
11, 2009.

BACKGROUND

[
3
]

Ms. Neufeld and Dr. Nesbitt are the parents of a
6-year old daughter.  Ms. Neufeld commenced an action in the Chilliwack
Registry, Action No. E5902, naming Dr. Nesbitt as a defendant.  Dr. Nesbitt, in
this proceeding, is represented by counsel.  Action No. E5902 relates to the
custody and access of their daughter.

[
4
]

The factual background of this action, commenced
by Dr. Nesbitt, relates to his and Ms. Neufeld’s ongoing dispute relating to
their daughter.

[
5
]

Ms. Neufeld commenced an action against Dr.
Nesbitt seeking damages for defamation.  This action was commenced in the New
Westminster Registry.

[
6
]

On April 30, 2009, Dr. Nesbitt filed in this
action a 164-paragraph statement of claim in which he purports Ms. Neufeld
wronged him in several ways.  Dr. Nesbitt claims damages for these alleged
wrongs.

[
7
]

On May 1, 2009, Dr. Nesbitt filed an amended
writ of summons.  He did not file an amended statement of claim.  In the
amended writ of summons, Dr. Nesbitt claims:

1)

False arrest.  Occurring on 23 Feb. 2006
resulting in two days imprisonment

2)

Malicious prosecution.  For trial on above
arrest, tried 8 Jan. 2007, and for which I was acquitted.

3)

Defamation of character.  Beginning in Nov. 2005
and continuing to the present time, in which the Plaintiff has been [falsely]
accused of being crazy, violent, a pedophile, of thieving, of being dangerous
to others , of stealing personal and professional property.

4)

Assault and battery.

5)

Abduction.

6)

Intentional infliction of emotional harm.

7)

Loss of consortium.

8)

Infliction of psychiatric injury.

9)

Infliction of economic loss.

10)

Harassment.

POSITIONS

Ms.
Neufeld

[
8
]

Ms. Neufeld alleges that Dr. Nesbitt’s statement
of claim discloses no reasonable claim (Rule 19(24)(a) of the
Rules
),
the pleadings have structural defects (Rule 19(24)(b) and (c) of the
Rules
)
and is an abuse of process (Rule 19(24)(d) of the
Rules
).

[
9
]

Further, the statement of claim is prolix and
refers to evidence offending Rule 19(1).  In addition, the statement of claim
includes conclusion of law without pleading the material facts on which it
relies.

[
10
]

Ms. Neufeld argues that the statement of claim
fails to establish a nexus between the alleged wrongs and quantifiable damages
to Dr. Nesbitt.

[
11
]

Ms. Neufeld alleges all of this makes it
impossible for her to understand the case she must meet.

Dr.
Nesbitt

[
12
]

Dr. Nesbitt’s position is that he has followed
the
Rules
and followed the instructions of self-help resources in
drafting his statement of claim.

THE LAW

[
13
]

The Rule 19 of the
Rules
are as follows:

Contents

(1) A pleading shall be as brief as the
nature of the case will permit and must contain a statement in summary form of
the material facts on which the party relies, but not the evidence by which the
facts are to be proved.

…

Pleading conclusions of law

(9.1)  Conclusions of law may be pleaded only if the
material facts supporting them are pleaded.

…

Where particulars necessary

(11)  Where the party pleading relies on
misrepresentation, fraud, breach of trust, wilful default or undue influence,
or where particulars may be necessary, full particulars, with dates and items
if applicable, shall be stated in the pleading. If the particulars of debt,
expenses or damages are lengthy, the party may refer to this fact and instead
of pleading the particulars shall deliver the particulars in a separate
document either before or with the pleading.

Particulars in libel or
slander

(12)  In an action for libel or slander,

(a) where the plaintiff
alleges that the words or matter complained of were used in a derogatory sense
other than their ordinary meaning, the plaintiff shall give particulars of the
facts and matters on which the plaintiff relies in support of that sense, and

(b) where the defendant
alleges that, in so far as the words complained of consist of statements of
fact, they are true in substance and in fact, and that in so far as they
consist of expressions of opinion, they are fair comment on a matter of public
interest, the defendant shall give particulars stating which of the words
complained of the defendant alleges are statements of fact and of the facts and
matters relied on in support of the allegation that the words are true.

…

Scandalous, frivolous or vexatious matters

(24)  At any stage of a proceeding the
court may order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of an
endorsement, pleading, petition or other document on the ground that

(a) it
discloses no reasonable claim or defence as the case may be,

(b) it is
unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c) it may
prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing or the proceeding, or

(d) it is
otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court
may grant judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may
order the costs of the application to be paid as special costs.

[
14
]

Section 3(2) of the
Limitation Act
reads
as follows:

Limitation periods

...

(2) After the expiration of 2 years
after the date on which the right to do so arose a person may not bring any of
the following actions:

(a) subject
to subsection (4) (k), for damages in respect of injury to person or property,
including economic loss arising from the injury, whether based on contract,
tort or statutory duty;

(b) for
trespass to property not included in paragraph (a);

(c) for
defamation;

(d) for
false imprisonment;

(e) for
malicious prosecution;

(f) for tort
under the Privacy Act;

(g) under
the Family Compensation Act;

(h) for
seduction;

(i) under section 27 of the Engineers and Geoscientists Act.

[
15
]

The British Columbia Court of Appeal in
Young
v. Borzoni,
2007 BCCA 16
, at para.
19
, stated the following test for
applications that seek to have statements of claims struck:

[19]
The Supreme Court of Canada set out in Odhavji Estate v.
Woodhouse,
2003 SCC 69 (CanLII)
, [2003] 3 S.C.R. 263 the test for striking out a statement
of claim on the basis that it disclosed no reasonable claim:

[14] ... a court
may strike out a statement of claim that discloses no reasonable cause of
action. The rules with respect to striking out a statement of claim are much
the same in other provinces. In British Columbia, for example, Rule 19(24)(a)
of the Rules of Court,
B.C. Reg. 221/90
, states that a court may strike out a
pleading on the ground that it discloses no reasonable claim.

[15] An excellent
statement of the test for striking out a claim under such provisions is that
set out by Wilson J. in Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959, at p. 980:

... assuming
that the facts as stated in the statement of claim can be proved, is it
"plain and obvious" that the plaintiff's statement of claim discloses
no reasonable cause of action? As in England, if there is a chance that the
plaintiff might succeed, then the plaintiff should not be "driven from the
judgment seat". Neither the length and complexity of the issues, the
novelty of the cause of action, nor the potential for the defendant to present
a strong defence should prevent the plaintiff from proceeding with his or her
case. Only if the action is certain to fail because it contains a radical
defect ... should the relevant portions of a plaintiff's statement of claim be
struck out ... .

The test is a stringent one. The facts are
to be taken as pleaded. When so taken, the question that must then be
determined is whether ... it is "plain and obvious" that the action
must fail. It is only if the statement of claim is certain to fail because it
contains a "radical defect" that the plaintiff should be driven from
the judgment.

[
16
]

I agree with Ms. Neufeld’s argument contained in
her outline dated September 3, 2009.  Dr. Nesbitt’s statement of claim is
prolix, and is little more than an irrelevant opinion of Dr. Nesbitt and
others, and events that have happened that have no relevance to the claims
being made.  On this basis alone, it could be struck out in its entirety (
Stephen
v. British Columbia (Ministry of Children & Family Development
),
2008
BCSC 1656
).

[
17
]

There are conclusions of law plead by Dr.
Nesbitt that do not set out any of the material facts on which he relies.  In
Delaney
& Friends Cartoon Productions Ltd.
,
2005 BCSC 371
, at para.
9
, Joyce J.
states:

A material fact
is one that is essential in order to formulate a complete cause of action. If a
material fact is omitted, a cause of action is not effectively pleaded.

[
18
]

Dr. Nesbitt has failed to plead the words or
actions that he alleges are defamatory in accordance with Rule 19(12) of the
Rules
.

[
19
]

Scandalous, frivolous, vexatious or embarrassing
pleadings have been defined by Joyce J. in
Stephen
:

[50]      In Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform
Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress (1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4th) 266 (BCSC) at para.

47
, Romilly J. summarized what must be established in order to find that
pleadings are "unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious" under
Rule 19(24)(b):

Irrelevancy and embarrassment are both
established when pleadings are so confusing that it is difficult to understand
what is being pleaded: Gittings v. Caneco Audio-Publishers Inc. (1987),
1987 CanLII 2561 (BC SC)
, 17
B.C.L.R. (2d) 38 (BCSC). An "embarrassing" and "scandalous"
pleading is one that is so irrelevant that it will involve the parties in
useless expense and will prejudice the trial of the action by involving them in
a dispute apart from the issues: Keddie v. Dumas Hotels Ltd. (1985),
1985 CanLII 417 (BC CA)
, 62
B.C.L.R. 145 (BCCA) at 147. An allegation which is scandalous will not be struck
if it is relevant to the proceedings. It will only be struck if irrelevant as
well as scandalous: College of Dental Surgeons (British Columbia) v. Cleland
(1968),
1968 CanLII 1008 (BC CA)
, 66 W.W.R. 499 (BCCA). A pleading is "unnecessary" or
"vexatious" if it does not go to establishing the plaintiff's cause
of action or does not advance any claim known in law: Strauts v. Harrigan
(December 2, 1991), Doc. Vancouver C913631 (BCSC). A pleading that is
superfluous will not be struck out if it is not necessarily unnecessary or
otherwise objectionable: Lutz v. Canadian Puget Sound Lumber
(1920), 28 B.C.R.
39 (BCCA)
. A pleading is "frivolous" if it is obviously
unsustainable, not in the sense that it lacks an evidentiary basis, but because
of the doctrine of estoppel: Chrisgian v. B.C. Rail Ltd. (July 3, 1992) Doc.
Prince George 20714 (B.C. Master).

[
20
]

Abuse of process is when a proceeding is being
used for some ulterior or improper purpose (
Budgell v. Oppal
,
2007 BCSC
991
).

[
21
]

I will assess Dr. Nesbitt’s statement of claim
in accordance with its headings and paragraphs.  I will not comment on each
paragraph.

The
Parties

[
22
]

Dr. Nesbitt’s and Ms. Neufeld’s respective
historical health problems stated in paragraphs 4 to 6 have no relevancy to the
various claims made by Dr. Nesbitt.

[
23
]

Paragraphs 7, 8, 11 and 12 are intended to
embarrass, as well are unnecessary to the statement of claim.

[
24
]

Paragraphs 13 to 18 are irrelevant.

Assault
and Battery

[
25
]

Paragraphs 19 and 20.  In paragraph 19, Dr.
Nesbitt does not allege when this event occurred.  He acknowledged, when making
his submissions, that this event is out of time and statute barred pursuant to
the
Statute of Limitations
.  Paragraph 20 has nothing to do with any of
the allegations against Ms. Neufeld and is irrelevant.

Intentional
Infliction of Emotional Harm and Defamation

[
26
]

Paragraphs 21 to 55 do not describe the
defamatory words, nor any particulars as required by Rule 19(12)(a) of the
Rules
.

[
27
]

Paragraphs 21 to 55 are allegations about Ms.
Neufeld and Dr. Nesbitt’s arrangements concerning their daughter’s visit with
Dr. Nesbitt.  The closest that Dr. Nesbitt comes to alleging defamatory words
are those alleged to have been spoken on February 5 (presumably in 2006), when
Dr. Nesbitt was called a “dead-beat dad.”  It was not alleged as to whom this
was stated, who was present and how it damaged Dr. Nesbitt.  Further, assuming
that it occurred in 2006, it is statute barred.

[
28
]

In paragraphs 50 to 54, Dr. Nesbitt sets out
inquiries he made as to why his access to his daughter is supervised and why it
is necessary.  None of this has anything to do with intentional infliction of
emotional harm or defamation.

[
29
]

Paragraphs 21 to 55 in the statement of claim
relate to the litigation over the custody and access of his daughter in Action
No.E5902, and the evidence that Dr. Nesbitt has to support his position in that
litigation.

False
Arrest and False Imprisonment

[
30
]

In paragraph 56 of the statement of claim, Dr.
Nesbitt alleges that Ms. Neufeld had him arrested and charged under
s. 810
of
the
Criminal Code
.

[
31
]

Dr. Nesbitt, in the statement of claim,
acknowledges that the police arrested and imprisoned him, not Ms. Neufeld.  He
blames Ms. Neufeld for these events.  As a result of all of this, Dr. Nesbitt
alleges he does not see his daughter.  Further, he alleges the event occurred
on February 21, 2006, making the claim statute barred.

[
32
]

In paragraphs 67 and 69, Dr. Nesbitt refers to
his health problems which have nothing to do with any claim against Ms. Neufeld
for false arrest and false imprisonment.

[
33
]

Dr. Nesbitt then launches into a description of
Ms. Neufeld’s evidence at his criminal trial in paragraph 71.  In paragraph 72,
Dr. Nesbitt quotes the Crown prosecutor and concludes at paragraph 73 that the
statement made by the Crown prosecutor meets the criteria for malicious
prosecution.  It does not.

[
34
]

In paragraph 74, Dr. Nesbitt claims that the
false arrest and imprisonment “caused Post Traumatic Stress Disorder type
symptoms, which are still persisting to this day.”  There is no connection
alleged to this event and any damages suffered by Dr. Nesbitt.

[
35
]

The allegations in paragraphs 75 to 108 relate
to Ms. Neufeld deleting emails of Dr. Nesbitt.  Dr. Nesbitt claims that in July
of 2005, Ms. Neufeld wrote emails in his name saying “derogatory things about
my relationships with women.” (paragraph 78).  The derogatory things are not
identified.  This event is also statute barred.

[
36
]

Dr. Nesbitt alleges that on July 3, 2005 and
October 16, 2005, and on other occasions not identified, Ms. Neufeld sent
emails to some named persons in Dr. Nesbitt’s name stating “derogatory things
about my relationships with and attitudes towards women.” (paragraph 79).  The
statements are not identified as to their content.  Further, both incidents are
statute barred.  These emails make no connection between the acts alleged and
any claim for damages.

[
37
]

In paragraphs 84 and 93 of the statement of
claim, Dr. Nesbitt sets out a series of unrelated events and evidence of what
Ms. Neufeld alleges that Dr. Nesbitt did, the evidence that Dr. Nesbitt has to
counter Ms. Neufeld’s allegations and how all of this may have affected his
access to his daughter.

[
38
]

In paragraphs 80 to 93, Dr. Nesbitt analyses the
need for two restraining orders and their being used to prevent him from seeing
his daughter.

[
39
]

Paragraphs 94 to 95 are an attempt to summarize
the evidence of professionals who have given opinions to the need of
supervision of Dr. Nesbitt when he exercises access to his daughter.

[
40
]

In paragraph 97, “the formal and informal
supervision has caused me both psychiatric injury and economic loss.”  There
are no particulars of these losses or damages.  It would appear that it is the
professional, Dr. England, who is recommending informal supervision and not Ms.
Neufeld.  Quoting other professional opinions, Dr. Nesbitt is attempting to
show other opinions that contradict that of Dr. England.  This evidence is
unrelated to the allegations of defamation.  It is obviously evidence that will
be used in the custody action.

[
41
]

Dr. Nesbitt, in paragraphs 106 to 108, alleges
that Ms. Neufeld defamed him by stating that he inappropriately dressed their
daughter and put lipstick on her, which he denies.  He then refers to specific
people who would give evidence stating that his daughter was not
inappropriately dressed by him.  Dr. Nesbitt does not state who or when these
events occurred.  It would appear that these are allegations which are the
subject matter of the custody and access action relating to his daughter.  Dr.
Nesbitt makes no claim he was damaged by these allegations.

Abduction

[
42
]

In paragraph 109, Dr. Nesbitt alleges that Ms.
Neufeld arranged to “have me ‘kidnapped’ by the supervisor” who on March 17,
2007 was supervising Dr. Nesbitt’s access with his daughter.  This kidnapping,
as alleged by Dr. Nesbitt, occurred when the supervisor returned to a different
parking lot than the usual parking lot for the return of his daughter to Ms.
Neufeld.  As this event occurred not with his consent or knowledge, this, Dr.
Nesbitt claims, is abduction.  According to Dr. Nesbitt, this affected his
plans to meet friends to go to a St. Patrick’s Day party and his plans to give
his daughter certain things he had in his car located in the other parking
lot.

[
43
]

Further on, in paragraphs 112 to 115, Dr.
Nesbitt describes certain events that occurred between him and Ms. Neufeld that
constituted breach of the restraining order.  He alleges that he has a video of
this entire event.

[
44
]

For a second time Dr. Nesbitt returns to the
heading “DEFAMATION AND INTENTIONAL INFLICTION OF EMOTIONAL HARM/PSYCHIATRIC
INJURY”.  Paragraphs 116 to 132 of the statement of claim are complaints of
cancellation of access to his daughter and false allegations about Dr.
Nesbitt’s behaviour with his daughter.  In addition, Dr. Nesbitt accuses Ms.
Neufeld of immoral behaviour.

[
45
]

In paragraphs 119 and 121, Dr. Nesbitt states
that in order to get Ms. Neufeld ‘oriented to reality’ he acknowledged that he
emailed members of Ms. Neufeld’s rotary club advising them of Ms. Neufeld and
her friends’ inappropriate behaviour.

[
46
]

The balance of the allegations relate to
websites described by Dr. Nesbitt referring to Ms. Neufeld and other people,
most of which makes no sense.  Further, Dr. Nesbitt analyses Ms. Neufeld
psychologically.

[
47
]

In paragraph 132 of the statement of claim, Dr.
Nesbitt states:

To assuage
Wendy’s false fears that I was libelling her I agreed to a Consent Order that I
would not distribute any information about Joyce Beal, Susan Elias, Wendy, her
brothers, or her father.  In spite of this Wendy started a Defamation Lawsuit
against me, threatening to go through with it unless I signed a declaration
agreeing to things which I had nothing to do with.

Wendy’s
Lawsuit Harassment

[
48
]

Paragraphs 133 to 135 relate to the law suit
that Ms. Neufeld filed against Dr. Nesbitt in the New Westminster Registry.
These have no place in this statement of claim, do not relate to the claims
that Dr. Nesbitt is making, and are matters that should be raised in that
particular action brought by Ms. Neufeld.

Terry
Voth and Molly

[
49
]

At paragraphs 136 to 147, Dr. Nesbitt accuses
Terry Voth, who is not a party to this action and who he alleges is Ms.
Neufeld’s common law husband, of conduct of which Ms. Neufeld complains of Dr.
Nesbitt.  Dr. Nesbitt states that he has complained of Mr. Voth’s behaviour to
the Ministry of Child and Family Services.  This and the other paragraphs set
out no reasonable cause of action and are obviously evidence that may be
referred to in the child custody action.

Denial of
Funeral, Recitals, Public Events, & Facebook

[
50
]

In paragraph 141, Dr. Nesbitt claims that as
part of a consent agreement that he signed, he stated he would not publically
mention Ms. Neufeld or her family members, which included Ms. Neufeld’s
father.  Ms. Neufeld’s father died.  Dr. Nesbitt travelled to attend the
funeral and was asked by a mutual family friend not to attend.  He asked a
friend to videotape his daughter singing at her grandfather’s funeral.  It
apparently was videotaped, and at the request of Ms. Neufeld, the tape was
erased.

[
51
]

Dr. Nesbitt then decided to post to his Facebook
page a eulogy that he wrote for Ms. Neufeld’s deceased father.  He complains
that Ms. Neufeld apparently had this removed, along with other pictures,
alleging that Ms. Neufeld said it was in violation of the consent order.  Dr.
Nesbitt claimed that Ms. Neufeld tried to have him arrested again.  There are
no particulars of when this happened and he states:

I view this as
her way of harassing me again, and once again by using the police.

[
52
]

Under the heading “Recitals” at paragraphs 149
to 159, Dr. Nesbitt accuses Ms. Neufeld of preventing him from attending events
that his daughter attends, both in public and private places.

[
53
]

In paragraph 162 of the statement of claim, Dr.
Nesbitt accuses Ms. Neufeld of harassment for the past several years,
particularizing those forms of harassment, which include the peace bond and the
restraining order granted by the courts.

[
54
]

In paragraph 163, Dr. Nesbitt alleges that Ms.
Neufeld inflicted emotional, physical harm and loss of consortium, psychiatric
injury and economic loss by insisting on supervised visits, restricting access
to his daughter.  Dr. Nesbitt also alleges that Ms. Neufeld refuses to submit
to a s. 15 assessment, restricting the places where Dr. Nesbitt takes his
daughter, training his daughter not to recognize him, insinuating that
affection between a father and daughter is wrong.  Finally, at paragraph 163
i., Dr. Nesbitt alleges:

Libelling and
slandering Patrick before mutual acquaintances and colleagues, the details of
which are scattered throughout this statement.

[
55
]

Loss of consortium is no longer a claim and has
been barred by statute.

[
56
]

Dr. Nesbitt’s statement of claim discloses no
reasonable claim, and if there are claims that could be resolved by amendments,
they are barred by the
Limitations Act
.  Some of the allegations are not
properly plead by not stating material facts on which they are based.  The
statement of claim is prolix and is an abuse of process.  It is for these
reasons I have struck Dr. Nesbitt’s statement of claim.

[
57
]

Under the heading “Remedies Sought”, Dr. Nesbitt
has claimed general damages but he has not described what damages he suffered
or connected them with any causes of action.  He has claimed aggravated damages
and punitive damages without establishing the cause of action in which he based
those claims.  There is no claim anywhere in the statement of claim as to
special damages.

COSTS

[
58
]

The financial statement of Dr. Nesbitt in the
custody and access action, discloses sufficient assets so, that at the very
least, Dr. Nesbitt could have sought advice as to the suitability of commencing
this action based on these pleadings.

[
59
]

It is obvious that paragraphs 2 to 164 of Dr.
Nesbitt’s statement of claim were intended to punish Ms. Neufeld.  The
statement of claim was a personal attack on Ms. Neufeld.  The statement of
claim names other parties who have nothing to do with the allegations that Dr.
Nesbitt makes against Ms. Neufeld, and who have nothing to do with any
reasonable cause of action.

[
60
]

Special costs may be awarded against a litigant
when the litigant’s conduct is “reprehensible” being misconduct deserving of
“reproof or rebuke” (
Garcia v. Crestbrook Forest Industries Ltd.
(1994),

1994 CanLII 2570 (BC CA)
, 9 BCLR (3d) 242 and
Young
).

[
61
]

I can only conclude that this action, as
depicted in the statement of claim, is intended to punish Ms. Neufeld for
bringing on the defamation action against Dr. Nesbitt and the events in the
child custody and access action.

[
62
]

I award special costs to Ms. Neufeld for this
application.

“H.C. Hyslop J.”

HYSLOP J.
